title: Hungry for right (Matthew 5:6)
hook: blessed are those who hunger and thirst for what is right

segments.voice: Yesterday, the meek: strength held gently, like a horse that takes the bridle. Did you hold back one sharp word? Day two hundred thirty-six.

Think of the hungriest you've ever been. Not a little peckish at four o'clock. Really hungry: a long hike, a fast, a day when everything went wrong and you forgot to eat. Or thirsty on a hot day, when water is all you can think about. Your whole body leans toward one thing. Now, what else in your life do you want like that? Most of us, if we're honest, want a lot of things that way. The fourth line of the sermon names one more.
screen: `THE HUNGRIEST YOU'VE EVER BEEN.` → `THIRSTY ON A HOT DAY.` → `WHAT ELSE DO YOU WANT LIKE THAT?`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled." Righteousness can sound like a stiff, churchy word. Someone who's righteous might be a little smug. But the Greek word, dikaiosune, is bigger and warmer than that. It means being right with God, and it also means justice: things being set right between people. Greek uses one word for both. So does Hebrew: tsedakah, which is also the Hebrew word Jews use for giving to the poor. So when Jesus says righteousness, his listeners could hear both: a heart right with God, and a world where the widow gets fed and the worker gets paid. The prophet Amos put it like this: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." Christians have leaned on one side or the other at different times, and many hold both together: personal holiness and public justice. Now notice the verbs. Not blessed are the righteous. Blessed are the hungry for it. People who don't have it yet, who ache for it the way you ache for water. That's hopeful. You don't have to be finished. You just have to want it badly. And the promise: they shall be filled. The Greek word for filled is a farmyard word, used for feeding animals until they're full. Matthew uses it again when five thousand people eat and are filled. Not a taste. A full meal.
screen: `DIKAIOSUNE: RIGHT, AND JUSTICE.` · `LIKE A MIGHTY STREAM.` · `BLESSED ARE THE HUNGRY FOR IT.` · `FILLED: A FULL MEAL.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL BE FILLED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one wrong you long to see righted. Settle, and breathe. Let something come to mind that isn't right. It could be big: hunger, a war, an injustice in the news. It could be close: a family rift, a friend treated unfairly, something you did. Choose one. Don't argue with it. Just let yourself feel the hunger for it to be made right. Notice where you feel it in your body. If you pray, you can offer that hunger to God. The bell holds the time.
Righteousness. Dikaiosune in Greek: being right with God and things set right between people, one word for both.
Your line: hunger for good. Today, feed that hunger once: one small act that sets something a little more right. Day two hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Christians pursue righteousness both in personal prayer and repentance and in works of justice and charity: food banks, advocacy for the poor, and giving, which many churches see as part of the same calling.

fork.setup: you hear this line and think: I'm nowhere near righteous. who does Jesus actually call blessed?
options: the ones who have achieved it.
the ones who hunger and thirst for it.
the ones who talk about it most.
fork.reveal: "Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness." wanting it, badly, is where the blessing starts.

original.note: Greek: righteousness, justice. one word for being right with God and setting things right.

trapdoor: what you thought: righteousness means being a good, proper person.
what it means: longing for things to be right, with God and between people.
what a scholar hears: dikaiosune and Hebrew tsedakah both mean righteousness and justice; filled is chortazo, to feed full.

notes: chortazo originally used of feeding animals with fodder: standard lexicon note; confirm. Matthew 14:20 uses it of the five thousand.
tsedakah as the Jewish term for charitable giving: confirm phrasing.
Christian emphases (personal holiness vs. public justice) described without ranking; confirm.
